al_nightmare_wall.blurb: A compact bolted wall in the Northeast Section of Buck's Pocket, on the Jackson County side of Sauty Creek in northeast Alabama. It is one of the first sport walls you come to in that section, just ahead of the Freebird buttress, at roughly 1,000 feet of elevation. Six sport routes share the wall, running from the low 5.10s through 5.11 with a single 5.12 at the top end, so it suits climbers who already lead steady 5.10 and want a few harder options. Other sport walls, trad lines and boulders sit nearby in the same section, which makes it easy to fold into a longer day.

al_big_boss_man_wall.blurb: A tall boulder at Smith Mountain, the bouldering area near Dadeville that holds most of the problems in central Alabama. This wall carries six problems and has the toughest set on the mountain: a handful of moderate V2 and V3 lines plus two serious outings at V6 and V8. Expect a step up in height and commitment compared with the smaller blocks nearby, so bring pads and spotters. It lies further along the trail that serves the fire tower boulders, and the mountain as a whole has several trails winding between its sub-areas.

al_the_dual_slit_boulder.blurb: A single boulder at Rainbow Mountain preserve in Madison, Alabama, offering six problems in a mix of styles. Most lines fall between V0 and V3, with one standout up around V6, so it works for newer boulderers and for someone wanting one hard project. You reach it by following the Balance Rock trail until you pass a pocketed roof and then a vertical wall. From the top of the nearby standable rock there is a good view over Madison. The preserve overall is known for short, easy walk-ins that suit an after-work session.

al_rainbow_warrior.blurb: A small, friendly boulder at Rainbow Mountain in Madison, Alabama, with six problems and an interesting off-width. The grades stay low, from V0 up to V3, with a couple at V2, which makes it a good stop for beginners and for warming up. The boulder stands right beside a trail sign where the Rainbow Mountain loop meets the Wild Trail, and a large crack splits its middle, so it is easy to spot. The whole preserve is a short-approach bouldering spot popular for quick sessions.

al_rainbow_ride.blurb: A lone boulder sitting in the woods beside a fallen tree at Rainbow Mountain in Madison, Alabama. Six problems are recorded, mostly V2 and V3 with one line up near V4, and a roof and a prow sit behind the downed tree. To find it, walk straight downhill from the leftmost parking spot toward a small cluster of boulders; the route in is only loosely described, so allow time to look around. It is a quiet corner of a preserve that is otherwise known for easy, short-walk bouldering.

al_near_side_cliffs.blurb: A stretch of short but solid cliffline in Hurricane Creek Park, Tuscaloosa, reached just beyond Roof Rock. It holds six boulder problems between V1 and V3, two at each grade, so it is a good fit for newer boulderers and for warming up. Some slabby, slopey lines are still possible here. The rocks are modest in height, and the cliffs are on your right as you keep walking the trail.
al_near_side_cliffs.approach: From the parking lot, follow the trail by the river past Roof Rock. The cliffline is on the right; if you reach a clearing where trees were cut, you have gone too far.
